chapters.name: Chapter 1: What big buyers want, and getting your farm ready

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What supermarkets, processors and exporters want
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List a big buyer's requirements and mark where your farm falls short.
This lesson builds toward: Given a supermarket, processor or export buyer's requirements, you will list what the buyer asks for and compare it with what your farm or group supplies now, covering volume, consistency, grade, traceability and food safety, with each gap marked.
Big buyers sell to customers who expect the same product, safe and on the shelf, every week. So they want five things from you: volume (enough to fill their orders), consistency (supply week after week, not just at harvest), grade (size, colour, ripeness and defects to their specification), traceability (they can find which farm and field a crate came from) and food safety (no harmful residues, germs or dirt).
Each buyer is different. A supermarket in Nairobi or Accra may want tomatoes in a set size and crate, delivered twice a week. A processor in Nigeria buying cassava for starch or tomatoes for paste wants large volumes at a set quality, and may care less about looks. An exporter shipping French beans from Kenya or mangoes from Senegal to Europe must meet the importing country's rules and often asks for a certificate.
Ask the buyer for their specification in writing. Then compare it, point by point, with what you supply now. The gaps you find are your work plan. Many small farms close the volume and consistency gaps by working as a group and staggering planting dates.
Step by step:
- Ask one buyer for their written specification and order size.
- List their needs under volume, consistency, grade, traceability and food safety.
- Next to each, write what your farm or group supplies now.
- Mark each gap and how you might close it (for example as a group or by staggered planting).
Words to know:
- Specification: the buyer's written description of the product they want: size, colour, ripeness, packing and defects allowed.
- Traceability: being able to follow produce back to the farm, field and inputs it came from.
- Consistency: supplying the same quality and amount, on time, again and again.
Try it now: Pick one big buyer near you (a supermarket, processor or exporter). Write their needs under the five headings, what you supply now next to each, and mark the gaps. This is the start of your buyer-readiness checklist.
You can now list what a big buyer wants and mark where your farm or group falls short.

check.q: A supermarket wants tomatoes every week all year. You harvest once a season. Which need do you miss?
check.why: Supplying every week, not just at harvest, is consistency.

check.q: What is the best way to know exactly what a buyer wants?
options: Guess from what is in their shop
Ask a neighbour who sold to them once
Send produce and see if they accept it
Ask for their specification in writing
check.why: A written specification shows the exact size, quality and packing the buyer will accept.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Good Agricultural Practices on your farm
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write the Good Agricultural Practices you will follow for one crop.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop on your farm, you will write the Good Agricultural Practices you will follow, covering registered pesticides used as the label says, protective equipment, the label's pre-harvest interval, clean water, hygiene at harvest and worker safety.
Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) are the farm habits that keep produce safe, protect workers and the environment, and make quality steady. Certification schemes and buyers audit them. You can start most of them for little money.
Pesticides: use only products registered by your national body (for example Kenya's Pest Control Products Board, Nigeria's NAFDAC or Ghana's EPA), check its current list, and use them exactly as the label says. Wear the protective equipment the label asks for, store chemicals locked away from food, and respect the label's pre-harvest interval, the waiting time between the last spray and harvest. Spraying too close to harvest is a main cause of residue rejections. Use integrated pest management so you spray less.
Also: clean water for spraying, washing and irrigation; clean harvest crates kept off the ground; toilets and handwashing for workers; no animals or manure near produce just before harvest; first aid and training for workers; and safe disposal of empty containers as the label or your national body says. Write these down as your farm's GAP rules.
Step by step:
- Check every pesticide you use is on your national body's register.
- Write the label's protective equipment and pre-harvest interval next to each product.
- Set up handwashing, toilets and clean crates for harvest.
- Write your GAP rules and train every worker on them.
Words to know:
- Good Agricultural Practices (GAP): farm habits that keep produce safe and protect workers and the environment.
- Pre-harvest interval: the waiting time on the label between the last spray and harvest.
- Registered pesticide: a product your national body has approved for that crop and use.
- Integrated pest management: controlling pests with several methods so you spray only when needed.
Official sources:
- FAO Pesticide Registration Toolkit: national pesticide registers in Africa
Try it now: Write your farm's GAP rules for one crop on one page: the registered pesticides you use with the label's protective equipment and pre-harvest interval, your water and harvest hygiene, and worker safety. Add the gaps to your buyer-readiness checklist.
You can now write Good Agricultural Practice rules for a crop, including safe, registered pesticide use.

check.q: Where do you find how long to wait between the last spray and harvest?
options: On the product label (the pre-harvest interval)
It does not matter for export
check.why: The label gives the pre-harvest interval; respecting it keeps residues within limits.

check.q: A trader offers a cheap pesticide with no registration number. What do you do?
options: Buy it if it is cheap
Mix it with a registered one
Do not use it; use only products on your national register
check.why: Unregistered products may be fake or banned and can cause rejections and harm.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Records that trace every crate
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up records that trace a crate back to its field, inputs and harvest date.
This lesson builds toward: For one season of one crop, you will set up traceability records that link each lot to its field, inputs and harvest date, so any crate can be traced back to the field and every spray within a few minutes.
If a buyer finds a residue or a problem, they will ask: which farm, which field, what was sprayed and when? Traceability records answer in minutes. Without them, a buyer may drop the whole group.
Give each field or plot a code, for example KB-F2 for Kiambu farm, field 2. Keep a spray and input record for each field: date, product name and registration number, amount, who sprayed and the pre-harvest interval from the label. Keep a harvest record: date, field code, crates or kilos, and a lot number. Write the lot number on every crate or delivery note.
Keep the records in a notebook or a simple phone spreadsheet, and keep receipts for inputs. Producer groups keep a member register and each member's records. Kenya is rolling out digital mapping and registration of export farms, so check with AFA what your crop needs.
Step by step:
- Give each field or plot a short code.
- Keep a spray and input record per field: date, product, registration number, amount, who sprayed, pre-harvest interval.
- Keep a harvest record with a lot number for each harvest.
- Write the lot number on every crate or delivery note.
- Practise: pick a crate and trace it back in minutes.
Words to know:
- Lot number: a code for one harvest from one field on one day, written on the crates.
- Spray record: a written list of every pesticide used: when, what, how much and by whom.
- Audit: a check by a buyer or certifier that you do what you say.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA), Horticultural Crops Directorate: export licences and registration (check current rules)
Try it now: Draw up the three records for one crop: field codes, a spray and input record, and a harvest record with lot numbers. Fill in one real or practice line in each, then trace that crate back to the field and the last spray.
You can now keep field, spray and harvest records that trace any crate back to its field and inputs.

check.q: What links a crate on the buyer's shelf to your field?
options: A lot number written on the crate and in your harvest record
check.why: A lot number on the crate and in your records traces it to the field and date.

check.q: Which detail belongs in a spray record?
options: Date, product, registration number, amount and who sprayed
The weather forecast for next month
check.why: These details show what was sprayed and when, which buyers and certifiers check.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Certification, export rules and supply contracts

lessons.title: Lesson 4: GLOBALG.A.P. and certification: cost and benefit
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare the costs and benefits of certification for your farm and choose a route.
This lesson builds toward: Given a certification such as GLOBALG.A.P., you will compare its costs and benefits for your farm or group and name the route you would take, naming the three cost elements, the steps to an audit and whether a group option fits.
Certification means an independent body checks your farm against a standard and gives you a certificate if you pass. GLOBALG.A.P. is the best-known farm standard asked for by many European supermarkets and exporters. Its Integrated Farm Assurance (IFA) standard for fruit and vegetables covers food safety and traceability, workers' health, safety and welfare, and the environment (water, fertilizer, pest management and plant protection products). Some buyers ask for other standards, such as organic or fair-trade schemes.
GLOBALG.A.P. says there are three cost elements: your own costs to get ready (training, toilets, chemical store, records); the certification body's fees for the audit and travel; and GLOBALG.A.P.'s registration and licence fees, which depend on your area and option. Audits are yearly and a certificate lasts one year. There is an option for producer groups, including smallholders, where one group certificate covers members who follow a shared quality system with internal inspections.
The steps: download the free rules and checklist, put the requirements in place, do a self-assessment, ask an approved certification body working in your country for an audit, fix any problems in the time given, and receive the certificate. Buyers can check certificates on GLOBALG.A.P.'s Supply Chain Portal. Before paying, ask your buyer: do you need this certificate, and will you buy more or pay more if I have it? Get quotes from more than one certification body.
Step by step:
- Ask your buyer which certificate, if any, they require.
- Download the standard's free rules and checklist and do a self-assessment.
- List the three cost elements and get quotes from approved certification bodies.
- Compare costs with the benefit: new buyers, more volume or a better price.
- Decide: certify alone, certify as a group, or not yet.
Words to know:
- Certification: an independent check that a farm meets a standard, proved by a certificate.
- Certification body: the approved company that audits your farm and issues the certificate.
- Group certification: one certificate for a producer group whose members follow a shared quality system.
- Self-assessment: checking your own farm against the standard's checklist before the real audit.
Official sources:
- GLOBALG.A.P.: Integrated Farm Assurance (IFA) for fruit and vegetables (topics, producer-group option, cost elements, steps to certification)
- GLOBALG.A.P.: Supply Chain Portal (check a certificate with the GLOBALG.A.P. number)
Try it now: For your crop and buyer, write a cost-benefit note on certification: does the buyer need it, the three cost elements (with quotes if you can get them), the benefit you expect, and your choice: alone, as a group, or not yet.
You can now compare the costs and benefits of a certification such as GLOBALG.A.P. and choose a route for your farm or group.

check.q: Which is one of GLOBALG.A.P.'s three cost elements?
options: The certification body's audit and travel fees
check.why: GLOBALG.A.P. lists your preparation costs, the certification body's fees, and its own registration and licence fees.

check.q: Twenty smallholders want certification but cannot each afford an audit. What may fit?
options: Group certification with a shared quality system
check.why: The producer-group option lets one certificate cover members who follow a shared system with internal inspections.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Residue limits, export rules and why shipments get rejected
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check the residue limits and export bodies that apply to your crop and market.
This lesson builds toward: Given a target export market, you will check the residue limits and the national export bodies that apply, naming where to find the limits (for example the EU Pesticides Database or Codex) and your country's export and plant-health bodies.
A maximum residue level (MRL) is the highest amount of a pesticide allowed to remain on a food. Each importing market sets its own. The European Union lists its limits in the EU Pesticides Database; Codex Alimentarius sets international limits that many countries use. A product can be legal at home and still be over the limit in Europe, or a pesticide may not be approved there at all.
This is not a small risk. Kenya's Agriculture and Food Authority linked a sharp fall in vegetable export earnings mainly to EU interceptions for pesticide residues, which rose from 25 cases in 2023 to 57 in 2024, and the EU increased checks on Kenyan beans and peas. Common causes: spraying too close to harvest, using a product not allowed in the market, wrong mixing, spray drift from a neighbour, and mixing produce from untraced farms.
Exports also need national approvals. In Kenya, the Horticultural Crops Directorate of AFA licenses exporters and registers agents, and KEPHIS issues phytosanitary certificates. In Nigeria, exporters register with the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC). In Ghana, exporters register with the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA). Plant-health inspection is done by each country's plant protection body. Rules change, so check each body before the season.
Step by step:
- Name your target market (for example the EU, the UK or a regional market).
- Look up the residue limits for your crop in that market's database or Codex.
- Check each pesticide you use is allowed there, and follow the label's pre-harvest interval.
- Ask your buyer whether residue tests are needed before shipping.
- List your country's export and plant-health bodies and what they require.
Words to know:
- Maximum residue level (MRL): the highest amount of a pesticide allowed to remain on a food in a market.
- Interception: when an importing country stops a shipment at the border because it breaks a rule.
- Phytosanitary certificate: an official paper saying a plant product is free of listed pests and diseases.
Official sources:
- European Commission: EU Pesticides Database (maximum residue levels by food and pesticide)
- Codex Alimentarius (FAO/WHO): international food standards, including pesticide residue limits
- Business Daily (KNBS data, AFA report): Kenya's vegetable export earnings down on EU pesticide rules; MRL interceptions rose from 25 (2023) to 57 (2024)
- Kenya Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA), Horticultural Crops Directorate: export licences and registration (check current rules)
- KEPHIS (Kenya): Phytosanitary services and export certification
- Nigerian Export Promotion Council: exporter e-registration
- Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA): register as an exporter
Try it now: For your crop and target market, find where the residue limits are listed and check two pesticides you use. Then list your country's export and plant-health bodies and one question to ask each. Add the results to your checklist.
You can now find the residue limits for your market and name the export and plant-health bodies you must deal with.

check.q: Your pesticide is registered in your country. Can produce still be rejected in Europe?
options: Yes, if residues are over the EU limit or the product is not allowed there
Only if the crates are dirty
check.why: Each market sets its own limits, so produce legal at home can break EU rules.

check.q: In Kenya, who issues phytosanitary certificates for exports?
check.why: KEPHIS handles plant-health inspection and phytosanitary certificates for Kenyan exports.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Meeting buyers, supply contracts and outgrower schemes
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a supply offer and list the contract terms you need from a buyer.
This lesson builds toward: Given a buyer meeting or an outgrower scheme offer, you will write a supply offer and the contract terms you need, stating grade, volume, schedule, price basis, rejection rules, payment terms and what happens if either side fails.
When you meet a buyer, come prepared: your crop, grade, how much you can supply and when, how you keep produce safe and traced, any certificate, and samples. Promise only what you can deliver. A missed delivery hurts trust more than a smaller offer.
Negotiate the terms, not just the price. Agree the grade and how it is checked, the volume and schedule, the price or how it is set (fixed, or linked to a market price), who pays transport and packing, the rejection rules (who checks, when, and what happens to rejected produce), the payment date and method, and what happens if your harvest fails or the buyer does not collect. Side-selling to another buyer breaks trust and often breaks the contract.
In an outgrower scheme, a company such as a processor or exporter contracts many small farmers, often giving seed, inputs, training or credit and buying the crop. It can open a steady market, but check: are inputs deducted from your payment and at what price, who sets the grade, what if prices rise, and can you leave? Read every contract fully, keep a copy, and ask a trusted adviser, extension officer or cooperative officer before you sign.
Step by step:
- Prepare your offer: crop, grade, volume, schedule, safety and traceability, certificate, samples.
- List the terms you need: grade check, price basis, transport, rejection rules, payment date, failure clauses.
- For an outgrower scheme, ask how inputs are charged, who grades, and how you can leave.
- Read the contract fully and ask a trusted adviser before signing.
- Keep a copy and deliver exactly what you promised.
Words to know:
- Supply offer: a written offer to a buyer of what you can supply, when and on what terms.
- Outgrower scheme: an arrangement where a company contracts many small farmers to grow for it, often giving inputs and buying the crop.
- Side-selling: selling contracted produce to another buyer.
- Rejection rules: the agreed rules for checking produce and what happens to produce the buyer refuses.
Try it now: Final task: finish your buyer-readiness checklist, marking what you meet and what you will fix. Then write a one-page supply offer to that buyer: crop and grade, volume and schedule, safety and traceability, certification, price basis and the contract terms you want.
You can now make a supply offer to a big buyer and list the contract terms that protect you, including in an outgrower scheme.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Buyer requirements and gaps The buyer's needs are vague, or gaps are not marked. Volume, consistency, grade, traceability and food safety are listed, with what you supply now and each gap marked. Based on the buyer's written specification, with a plan and date to close each gap. Good Agricultural Practices No written GAP rules, or unregistered pesticides or no protective equipment. Written rules: registered pesticides used as labelled, protective equipment, pre-harvest interval, water, harvest hygiene and worker safety. Workers have been trained and the rules are posted where they work. Traceability records No field codes, spray record or lot numbers. Field codes, a spray and input record and a harvest record with lot numbers; one crate can be traced back. Records are kept for the whole group and a trace test was done in a few minutes. Certification and export rules Certification is assumed or ignored, or no export bodies named. A cost-benefit note names the three cost elements and a route (alone, group or not yet). Includes real quotes from certification bodies and the buyer's answer on whether it is needed. Residue limits No check of the market's residue limits. Names where the limits are listed and checks the pesticides used against them, plus the export and plant-health bodies. Has asked the buyer or a lab about residue testing before shipping. Supply offer and terms No offer, or it promises more than the farm or group can deliver. A one-page offer with grade, volume, schedule, safety, certificate, price basis and the contract terms wanted. Includes rejection rules, failure clauses and payment terms, and was shown to an adviser. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the checklist or offer and try again.

check.q: Which term protects you if the buyer refuses part of a delivery?
options: Clear rejection rules: who checks, when, and what happens to refused produce
check.why: Rejection rules prevent unfair refusals and say who bears the loss.

check.q: An outgrower company gives seed and fertilizer on credit. What should you ask first?
options: How the inputs are priced and deducted from your payment
check.why: Input charges can take much of your payment, so know the price and how it is deducted.
